explanation: Processor pipelining improves instruction execution speed by overlapping the execution stages of multiple instructions.  However, this can lead to hazards (data, control, or structural) that require handling to maintain correct program execution. Data hazards occur when an instruction depends on the result of a previous instruction that hasn't completed yet. Control hazards arise from branch instructions, where the next instruction to execute is unknown until the branch condition is evaluated. Structural hazards occur when multiple instructions require the same hardware resource simultaneously. Hazard handling techniques include data forwarding (to avoid stalls due to data hazards), branch prediction (to reduce stalls due to control hazards), and pipeline design modifications (to mitigate structural hazards).
syntax: No single syntax; pipeline stages (e.g., Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback) are interconnected with forwarding paths and hazard detection/resolution logic.
example_explanation: This simplified example shows a 5-stage pipeline.  Each stage performs a specific part of instruction execution.  A real pipeline would be far more complex, including hazard detection and resolution logic. For example, data forwarding would involve checking dependencies between consecutive instructions and forwarding results from the EX or MEM stages to the EX stage of a subsequent instruction, preventing stalls if a dependency is detected. Branch prediction would involve predicting the outcome of a branch instruction and speculatively fetching instructions along the predicted path.  These mechanisms are crucial for mitigating hazards and achieving the performance benefits of pipelining.
